summary: Extends the Point-to-Point Protocol with a new encapsulation called Simple Data Link (SDL) for carrying multi-protocol datagrams over point-to-point links, including SONET/SDH circuits. It offers a lower-overhead alternative to HDLC-like framing. It is an experimental protocol.

eli5.summary: Data sent over a wire gets wrapped in a package. This proposes a lighter package that wastes less space, so more of the wire carries the real message.

subtitle: A low-overhead frame format for PPP over high-speed fiber links

tldr.problem: PPP over SONET/SDH using standard HDLC-like framing has high overhead: at least 7 octets per frame plus the possibility of 100% data overhead in the worst case, leaving less bandwidth for actual data.
tldr.mechanism: SDL (Simple Data Link) provides a fixed 4-octet header per frame with zero data overhead, followed by the PPP packet and a 4-octet CRC. The header contains only the packet length and a check code, allowing simple hardware framing and positive synchronization detection.
tldr.outcome: PPP over SDL offers significantly higher throughput and lower equipment cost for SONET/SDH lines. The RFC specifies SDL framing procedures, CRC generation, error correction, and LCP options for PPP to negotiate SDL encapsulation on SONET/SDH circuits.

today: RFC 2823 is an Experimental protocol and has not been updated or obsoleted. It saw limited adoption in the late 1990s and early 2000s for some high-speed carrier circuits, but most deployments continued to use standard HDLC-like framing on SONET/SDH. Modern equipment increasingly uses other protocols (such as Ethernet over SONET) for data transport over optical networks.

sections.title: Framing Over SONET and SDH Circuits
sections.content:
The Point-to-Point Protocol (PPP) is designed to carry multi-protocol datagrams over point-to-point links. RFCs 1662 and 2615 define how to carry PPP over SONET/SDH circuits using Octet Synchronous (O-S) framing with HDLC-like flag bytes and octet stuffing.

However, O-S framing on SONET/SDH has high overhead: each PPP frame is surrounded by flag bytes (7-octet overhead minimum), and data bytes containing certain bit patterns must be escaped, which can double the data size in the worst case. This means that even on a gigabit SONET link, a significant fraction of the bandwidth is consumed by framing, not data.

This RFC introduces SDL (Simple Data Link) as an alternative encapsulation. SDL is defined in a separate Lucent specification and was originally designed for raw fiber. This document adapts SDL to work with PPP over SONET/SDH, providing a much lower-overhead alternative to HDLC-like framing while maintaining positive frame synchronization.
sections.eli5: When you mail a letter, the envelope and address take up space. The original way sends big envelopes. SDL proposes tiny envelopes so more of each package is the actual letter.

sections.title: SDL Frame Structure and Packet Length
sections.content:
Each PPP packet in SDL is preceded by a fixed 4-octet header and followed by a 4-octet CRC. The header contains a 16-bit packet length field and a 16-bit CRC to protect the header itself. The packet length field indicates the number of octets in the PPP packet (including address and control fields) but not including the CRC.

The header is DC-balanced by XORing it with a 32-bit Barker-like sequence (B6AB31E0 hex). This ensures that the header does not introduce imbalances in the DC component of the signal on the line, which is important for SONET/SDH transmission.

PPP packets with fewer than 4 octets are padded to 4 octets. Idle time is filled with headers having a packet length of zero (4 octets). Special messages (scrambler state, A/B messages) use packet lengths of 1 to 3 and occupy 12 octets total.

The PPP packet and its 4-octet CRC are scrambled using an independent self-synchronous x^43+1 scrambler (the same polynomial used in ATM). The header is not scrambled. The CRC is a 32-bit ITU-T polynomial with initial value FFFFFFFF and is transmitted in network byte order.
sections.eli5: Each packet gets a small label saying how many bytes come next, then the real data, then a check number. The label is encoded so the signal stays balanced on the wire.

sections.title: Frame Synchronization and Error Correction
sections.content:
The SDL receiver must locate the start of frames in the continuous data stream. It does this using a state machine similar to ATM HEC delineation. The receiver searches for a valid 4-octet sequence with a correct CRC-16 header check code, entering HUNT state. Once a valid header is found, the receiver enters PRESYNCH state. If a second valid header is found at the expected location (based on the first header's packet length), the receiver enters SYNCH state and begins passing PPP data to the upper layers.

Once synchronized, single-bit errors in the SDL header can be corrected using a Galois field error correction technique based on the CRC residue. The receiver maintains an 8-octet (64-bit) syndrome lookup table to identify which bit (if any) is in error. Multiple-bit errors in the header are detected but not corrected; any uncorrectable error returns the link to HUNT state.

The RFC defines performance metrics for SDL synchronization: Mean Time to Frame, Mean Time to Synchronization, Probability of False Frame, Probability of False Synchronization, and Probability of Loss of Frame. These depend on the packet size distribution and error rate of the underlying SONET/SDH circuit.
sections.eli5: The receiver hunts through the data looking for a valid label, then checks the next label appears in the right place. Once it is sure, it starts listening. If a single bit gets corrupted in a label, it can fix it, but if two bits are wrong, it stops and hunts again.

sections.title: LCP Negotiation and Scrambler Modes
sections.content:
Two methods enable SDL on a PPP link: LCP negotiation and prior arrangement. The RFC defines a new LCP Configuration Option (Type 29) to request SDL operation. LCP-capable systems MUST be able to change the SONET/SDH Path Signal Label (PSL) value and detect the peer's value. When SDL is negotiated by LCP, both sides start in standard O-S framing mode on PSL value 22 or 207, exchange the SDL LCP option, and then switch to SDL framing once an SDL option is received.

The prior-arrangement method allows two endpoints to be pre-configured for SDL without LCP negotiation. This is useful where equipment cannot support PSL value changes or when operating with legacy SDH monitoring equipment that would misinterpret a PSL change as a failure.

For scrambler operation, the RFC defines two modes: self-synchronous (the default) and set-reset (optional). The self-synchronous scrambler is a 43-stage shift register initialized to all-ones and maintained purely by data itself. An optional set-reset scrambler provides an alternative for environments where the self-synchronous scrambler may cause problems (such as the 'killer packet' problem: a specific input pattern that causes unwanted scrambler behavior).
sections.eli5: Two routers can agree to use SDL by sending each other a preference message, or they can be pre-configured to use it without asking. There are two ways to scramble the data: one that syncs itself, and one that needs a reset message.

sections.title: Overhead and Throughput Benefits
sections.content:
SDL achieves its efficiency gains through a minimal header format. The fixed overhead per frame is 8 octets (4-octet header plus 4-octet CRC) plus the PPP packet length. There is zero data overhead (no octet stuffing or escape sequences), whereas HDLC-like framing with octet stuffing can require up to 100% data overhead in the worst case.

For a typical PPP frame of 1500 octets, O-S framing adds at least 7 octets plus potential stuffing overhead. SDL adds exactly 8 octets. For a full-duplex gigabit SONET link carrying maximum-size PPP frames, SDL reduces the framing overhead from approximately 0.5% to 0.5%, but more significantly, it reduces buffer requirements and hardware complexity because the receiver does not need to handle escape sequences.

The RFC includes performance analysis showing Mean Time to Frame measured in packets (not bits), which depends on the probability of false frame detection and the distribution of frame sizes. For typical packet sizes, SDL achieves rapid synchronization (under one thousand packets) even with relatively high bit error rates.
sections.eli5: Every packet costs 8 bytes of labels instead of up to 7 plus doubling the size with escaping. On big pipes with big packets, SDL wastes much less space on overhead.

sections.title: Compatibility and Configuration
sections.content:
The RFC specifies PSL values 23 and 25 for SDL operation: value 23 for SDL with self-synchronous scrambler (the default) and value 25 for SDL with set-reset scrambler. These values are allocated by ANSI T1X1.5 and ITU-T and appear in standards documents like T1.105 and G.707.

SDL implementations MUST support LCP negotiation if they support PSL value changes. All SDL implementations MUST support CRC-32 (4 octets) and MUST reject any LCP FCS Alternatives Option that requests a different CRC size while in SDL mode. The RFC permits optional support for other CRC types only through prior arrangement.

An implementation-specific configuration option SHOULD allow administrators to choose between LCP-negotiated and prior-arrangement modes. The default SHOULD be LCP-negotiated if the hardware supports PSL changes; otherwise, it MUST default to prior-arrangement mode. This ensures compatibility with SDH monitoring equipment that may not handle PSL changes gracefully.
sections.eli5: SDL fits into the standards for fiber transmission, and routers can either ask each other to use it or be told beforehand to use it. Once it is on, both sides must use the same checksum size and cannot change it mid-conversation.
